Ammonia synthesis

Industrial ammonia synthesis proceeds over an iron catalyst at high pressure and moderate temperature, combining nitrogen and hydrogen gas. The reaction is exothermic and reversible.mw-ref-never-shown

Reaction equation

The overall balanced equation for the Haber–Bosch route is written below.

N + 3 H \mathrm{N_2 + 3H_2} \rightarrow \mathrm{2NH_3}
Catalystinfobox-never-shown
  • Nitrogen sourced from air
  • Hydrogen sourced from methane reforming

Industrial conditions

Plant-scale reactors run continuously, recycling unreacted gas back through the converter bed. A typical single train operates several parallel catalyst baskets in series, with intercooling between beds to pull the exothermic reaction back toward a favourable equilibrium at each stage.

Feed gas purity matters more than raw throughput: trace sulfur and oxygen compounds poison the iron catalyst irreversibly, so upstream purification trains are sized generously even though they add capital cost without adding nameplate output.

Yield optimisation

Le Chatelier's principle guides the choice of pressure and temperature ranges; the équilibre constant sets a hard ceiling on per-pass yield regardless of catalyst quality. Operators trade higher pressure (better yield, more compression cost) against lower temperature (better yield, slower kinetics), settling on a compromise that varies by plant vintage.

  • Older plants: lower pressure, larger catalyst volume
  • Modern plants: higher pressure, smaller footprint
  • Recycle loops recover unreacted nitrogen and hydrogen after each pass
